summary: GTDD separates a testing agent that generates new adversarial inputs after each candidate implementation is committed from the coding agent, with a trusted reference evaluator returning reduced counterexamples that become regression tests, and an independent random audit deciding acceptance. Most of the paper is finite-population theory bounding false acceptance under adaptive development; a small paired experiment on one Redis-like key-value store with gpt-4.1-mini shows regenerating tests each round beats tests generated once by the same LLM, but not a property-based baseline drawn from the evaluation distribution.

claims.claim: Policies that regenerate tests each repair round end with lower failure rates than tests generated once by the same LLM.
claims.evidence: Table 6: Dynamic informed - Static LLM = -0.131, 95% CI [-0.228,-0.050], p=0.0015, 19/7 blocks; Dynamic blind - Static LLM = -0.126. Text admits the mean is driven by three blocks where Static LLM broke its module; median difference -0.044, trimmed mean -0.076, sign test p=0.029. Dynamic policies also requested more traces (600 vs 400).

claims.claim: Giving the tester the candidate's source gives no detectable additional improvement.
claims.evidence: Table 6: Dynamic informed - Dynamic blind = -0.005, CI [-0.044,+0.034], p=0.810 (30 blocks; null result, low power).

claims.claim: The study cannot attribute the advantage to regeneration, trace count, or counterexample history alone.
claims.evidence: Four post hoc added conditions (Static LLM 600 0.355, Staged 600 0.311, Regenerated without history 0.297, Blind rerun 0.308) show no detectable adjacent differences; Blind rerun vs Static LLM 600 CI [-0.121,+0.037].

claims.claim: Fresh random audits after candidate commitment control false acceptance across rounds.
claims.evidence: Theorems 4.10-4.15 with proofs; applied to the 600 recorded candidates: 83-case zero-failure audit gives 0.074 expected false acceptances over 150 trajectories. Only 1 of 150 trajectories reached failure rate <=0.01.

claims.claim: Dynamic adversarial testing beats conventional property-based testing.
claims.evidence: Not supported: Dynamic informed - Static property = -0.024, CI [-0.097,+0.043], p=0.534. Paper itself says no detectable advantage.

patterns.note: Static LLM-written tests up front were not better than public-example-only (+0.064, n.s.); regenerated tests helped, property tests matched them.
Execution against a trusted reference with reduced counterexample feedback lowered failure from 0.548 to ~0.27 over four rounds.
Requires a human-specified behavioral contract (2,072-word spec fixing every reply and error code) plus input schema; the protocol depends on it.
Spec plus reference implementation as the oracle; argues acceptance must be separated from development feedback.
Separate tester/coder roles; separation via source access showed no measurable benefit.
Acceptance via independent random audit rather than visible tests; humans set contract and tolerance.

methodology.sample: One task (61-command in-memory key-value store), 30 paired blocks, 5 original + 4 post hoc conditions, 4 coding rounds; 2,000-trace private evaluation set.
methodology.baselines: Public only, Static property (400 traces from the evaluation generator, a strong baseline), Static LLM (one generator before development).
methodology.models: gpt-4.1-mini (2025-04-14) as both coder and tester, single requests, no tool access, API default temperature.
methodology.variance: Block bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples), sign-flip permutation p-values, medians/trimmed means; secondary contrasts not multiplicity-adjusted.
methodology.ablations: Source access, trace count, staging, regeneration, history (post hoc, exploratory).
methodology.contamination_controls: Evaluation traces never shown to either model; custom spec reduces memorization risk.
methodology.languages: Python implementation (candidates imported into evaluator process; Python equality issue discussed).

standards.artifacts: No code or data link found in the text.
standards.preregistration: No; primary comparison declared, added conditions explicitly post hoc.

biases.detail: Only gpt-4.1-mini, used as both coder and tester.
Single synthetic Redis-subset task with a 620-line reference implementation; no repository-scale code.
Candidates are Python modules run in the evaluator process.
30 blocks; mean effect driven by three blocks where Static LLM broke the module.
No code, prompts, or records release found.
Coder is a single API request without tool access, unlike real coding agents; author lists this as a deviation from the protocol (§6).

verdict_reason: Unusually honest statistics and a useful acceptance-vs-feedback separation, but empirical support is one toy task, one small model, no tools, no artifacts; property tests matched the proposed method.
applicability: Directly relevant to spec-driven rollout: write a behavioral contract plus input schema for each ingestion endpoint or content transformation, generate fresh tests from it after each agent commit, turn every discovered counterexample into a stored regression test, and keep the acceptance gate separate (a hidden or freshly sampled audit set the coding agent never sees). For a Java team the cheapest strong option the paper supports is property-based testing (jqwik/junit-quickcheck) drawn from the real input distribution, since dynamic LLM testers did not beat it. Requires a trusted oracle; for domain data that may mean a reference transformer or golden content fixtures per repo. Host-agnostic, but nothing here covers cross-repo contracts across the several repositories or Java-specific evidence.

conflicts_with.detail: TDD-Agent reports gains from generating tests first then refining; here LLM tests generated once before development did not beat public-example-only (+0.064, n.s.) and only per-round regeneration helped.
